reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry reads the two commands as sequential appointments — first to Galilee, then to a later Jerusalem gathering before the ascension.

discrepancy.connective: Dale Allison presses the sharper reading: Luke-Acts and Matthew-Mark preserve two independent, incompatible resurrection traditions that no unmentioned Galilee side-trip can reconcile.

skeptic.name: Dale C. Allison Jr.
skeptic.work: Resurrecting Jesus: The Earliest Christian Tradition and Its Interpreters
skeptic.attribution: Dale C. Allison Jr., Resurrecting Jesus: The Earliest Christian Tradition and Its Interpreters (T&T Clark, 2005), pp. 260-269.

excerpts.excerpt_text: In Jerusalem Christ, by his angel, had appointed his disciples to meet him in Galilee; there he appointed them to meet him in Jerusalem again, such a day.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: MHC reads Jesus's Galilee summons (Matt 28:10/Mark 16:7) and his later 'do not depart from Jerusalem' order (Luke 24:49/Acts 1:4) as two separate, sequential appointments rather than one contradictory command.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing (Matt. 28:10, 16 vs. Luke 24:49) under 'Historical Discrepancies,' arguing the Jerusalem command meant 'make Jerusalem your head-quarters' and would not preclude a brief Galilee excursion, and noting (citing Alford) that the command may not have been given until after the Galilee visit.

link.title: Luke 24:49—Why did the disciples go to Galilee when Jesus commanded them to stay in Jerusalem?
link.note: live apologetic treatment paralleling Haley's chronological-sequence argument
